Write both fields from the standard axial formula and take the ratio.
**Step 1 — the field at the centre.**
B_c = **µ₀I/(2r)** ✓
**Step 2 — the field on the axis at distance x.**
B_a = µ₀Ir²/[2(r² + x²)^(3/2)] ✓
**Step 3 — set x = r.**
(r² + r²)^(3/2) = (2r²)^(3/2) = **2√2 r³** ✓
so
B_a = µ₀Ir²/(2 x 2√2 r³)
= **µ₀I/(4√2 r)**
**Step 4 — form the ratio.**
B_c/B_a = [µ₀I/(2r)] x [4√2 r/(µ₀I)]
= 4√2/2
= **2√2** ✓
**Step 5 — state it.** B_c : B_a = **2√2 : 1** ✓
**Step 6 — evaluate.** 2√2 = **2·83**, so the centre field is nearly three times the
axial field one radius away ✓
**Why the field falls off so quickly.** The denominator carries the power **3/2** ✓
Even at x = r the field has already dropped to 35% of its central value, and far away
it goes as **1/x³** - the dipole law.
**A check at the two ends of the formula.**
x = 0: B = µ₀Ir²/(2r³) = **µ₀I/(2r)** ✓ the central value, as it must be
x ≫ r: B ≈ µ₀Ir²/(2x³) = µ₀(2m)/(4πx³) with m = IπR² ✓ the standard dipole field.
**Why the field is strongest at the centre.** Every element of the loop is at the same
minimum distance r, and all their contributions add along the axis ✓ Move away and each
element is further off and contributes at an angle, so the resultant falls.
**A useful landmark.** The field has dropped to **half** its central value at
x = 0·766r ✓ so the loop's field is appreciable only within about a radius of it - which
is why Helmholtz coils use **two** loops to make a uniform region.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 2√2** ✗ inverts the ratio, making the axial field the
stronger - impossible. **√2 : 1** ✗ and **1 : √2** ✗ drop the factor of 2 from the
(2r²)^(3/2) ✓
∴ 2√2 : 1.

Apply F̄ = qv̄ x B̄, remembering that the **electron's charge is negative** and that a
**neutron is uncharged**.
**Step 1 — set up directions.** The particles enter moving **upward** (+ŷ) and the field
is **into the page** (−ẑ) ✓
**Step 2 — find v̄ x B̄.**
ŷ x (−ẑ) = **−x̂** - pointing **left** ✓
**Step 3 — apply the charges.**
**proton** (+e): F̄ = +e(−x̂) → deflects **left** ✓
**electron** (−e): F̄ = −e(−x̂) = **+x̂** → deflects **right** ✓
**alpha** (+2e): deflects **left**, like the proton but with a **smaller** radius
**neutron** (no charge): **no force**, so it goes **straight** ✓
**Step 4 — match to the tracks.** The figure shows A and B curving **left**, C going
**straight up**, and D curving **right** ✓ So the **electron follows track D**.
**Step 5 — identify the others.** C is the **neutron** ✓ and of the two left-curving
tracks, the one with the **smaller radius** is the alpha particle, since
r = mv/(qB) ✓ and the alpha's m/q is 2 against the proton's 1 - so in fact the alpha's
radius is **twice** the proton's, and the more sharply curved left track is the proton.
**Why the electron curves so sharply.** Its m/q is **1/1836** of the proton's ✓ so its
radius is minute - which is consistent with D being drawn as the tightest curve of all.
**The key discriminator.** The **sign** of the charge decides **which way** the track
bends; the **m/q ratio** decides **how sharply** ✓ Two independent pieces of
information, read from one photograph - which is exactly how particle physicists
identify tracks in a bubble chamber.
**Why the neutron proves the point.** It passes undeflected, confirming that the
deflection is **magnetic** and not caused by anything else in the apparatus ✓
**The speed is unchanged for all of them.** A magnetic force does **no work**, so each
charged particle keeps its speed and merely turns ✓
**Reading the distractors.** Tracks **A** and **B** ✗ bend the way a **positive**
charge must. Track **C** ✗ is the uncharged neutron ✓
∴ D.

The straight wire's field at the loop is **parallel to the loop's own current**, so the
cross product - and the force - vanishes.
**Step 1 — find the field of the straight wire.** A long straight conductor produces
field lines that are **circles concentric with it** ✓ With the wire along the loop's
axis, those circles lie in planes perpendicular to the axis - the same planes as the
loop itself.
**Step 2 — see how that field meets the loop.** At every point of the loop, the wire's
field B̄ points **tangentially**, along the circle ✓ The loop's current element Id̄l̄
also points tangentially, along the same circle.
**Step 3 — compute the force.**
dF̄ = I d̄l̄ x B̄ ✓
With d̄l̄ **parallel** to B̄ at every point, the cross product is **zero** everywhere:
**F = 0** ✓
**Why the symmetry makes this inevitable.** The arrangement is perfectly symmetric about
the axis ✓ Any force on the loop would have to point in some particular direction - but
no direction is singled out, so the net force must vanish. The detailed calculation
merely confirms what the symmetry already guarantees.
**Is there a torque?** No ✓ For the same reason: a torque would need a preferred axis,
and the symmetry provides none. The loop neither moves nor turns.
**The companion case.** Put the straight wire **parallel to the loop's plane**, outside
it, and the situation changes completely ✓ The field is then perpendicular to parts of
the loop, the forces no longer cancel, and the loop is both pushed and twisted.
**What the loop does to the wire.** By Newton's third law, also **nothing** ✓ The loop's
field at the axis is along the axis, parallel to the wire's current, so again
Id̄l̄ x B̄ = 0.
**The practical significance.** A coil wound coaxially around a current-carrying rod
feels no force from it ✓ which is why coaxial arrangements are mechanically stable -
an important consideration in high-current apparatus.
**Reading the distractors.** Forces **in the plane of the loop**, towards or away from
the centre ✗ would be radial, and the cross product gives nothing radial here. A force
**perpendicular to the plane** ✗ would require a radial field component, which a wire
along the axis does not produce ✓
∴ zero.

The magnetic force is **qv̄ x B̄**, which needs motion **and** a component of B
perpendicular to that motion.
**Step 1 — write the force.**
F̄ = q(v̄ x B̄), with magnitude **qvB sin θ** ✓
**Step 2 — see what makes it vanish.**
**v = 0**: no motion, so **F = 0** whatever the field ✓
**θ = 0 or 180°**: velocity **parallel** to B, so sin θ = 0 and **F = 0** ✓
**Step 3 — see what maximises it.**
**θ = 90°**: velocity **perpendicular** to B, giving the greatest possible force
**F = qvB** ✓
**Step 4 — test the four statements.**
"**moving, B perpendicular to velocity**" ✓ **correct** - the maximum-force case
"**moving, B parallel to velocity**" ✗ gives zero
"**stationary, B perpendicular**" ✗ gives zero, since v = 0
"**stationary, B parallel**" ✗ gives zero twice over
**Why a stationary charge feels nothing.** Magnetism acts on **moving** charge ✓ A
charge at rest in a magnetic field is entirely unaffected - which is the sharpest
distinction between magnetic and electric forces, since an electric field acts on a
charge whether it moves or not.
**Why a parallel velocity gives nothing.** A cross product vanishes between parallel
vectors ✓ A charge shot straight along a field line continues in a straight line at
constant speed, feeling no force at all.
**What happens in between.** For a general angle the velocity splits into a component
**along** B, which is unaffected, and a component **across** it, which circles ✓ The
resulting path is a **helix**.
**Why the force does no work.** It is always perpendicular to v̄, so F̄·v̄ = 0 ✓ A
magnetic field can change a particle's **direction** but never its **speed** - which is
why a cyclotron needs an electric field to accelerate and a magnetic field only to
steer.
**The full Lorentz force.**
F̄ = q(Ē + v̄ x B̄) ✓
The electric part acts always; the magnetic part only on moving charge, and only
perpendicular to its motion.
∴ the particle is moving and magnetic field is perpendicular to the velocity.

A velocity with components both along and across the field gives a **helix**.
**Step 1 — split the velocity.**
v_∥, **parallel** to B̄
v_⊥, **perpendicular** to B̄ ✓
**Step 2 — follow each component.**
the **parallel** part feels **no force**, since v̄ x B̄ vanishes for parallel vectors, so
it continues **unchanged** at constant speed ✓
the **perpendicular** part feels a force qv_⊥B, always at right angles to itself, so it
traces a **circle** ✓
**Step 3 — combine them.** A circle in the plane perpendicular to B, advancing steadily
along B - that is a **helix** ✓
**The parameters of the helix.**
radius: r = **mv_⊥/(qB)** ✓
period: T = **2πm/(qB)** - independent of the speed
pitch (the advance per turn): p = v_∥T = **2πmv_∥/(qB)** ✓
**A worked instance.** An electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ entering a 0·01 T field at 30°:
v_⊥ = 5 x 10⁵, v_∥ = 8·66 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹
r = **2·8 x 10⁻⁴ m**, T = **3·6 x 10⁻⁹ s**, pitch = **3·1 x 10⁻³ m** ✓
**Why the speed never changes.** The magnetic force does **no work** ✓ The helix is
traced at constant speed, with the velocity's direction rotating about the field
direction.
**The two limiting cases.**
v_∥ = 0: the pitch is zero and the helix collapses to a **circle** ✓
v_⊥ = 0: the radius is zero and the path is a **straight line** along B ✓
The helix is the general case that contains both.
**Where helical motion matters.** Charged particles from the Sun spiral along the
Earth's field lines towards the poles, producing the **aurora** ✓ The same spiralling
confines plasma in a tokamak and guides electrons in a magnetron.
**Why not an ellipse.** An elliptical path would need a force varying with position,
like the inverse-square force of gravity ✓ Here the magnetic force has constant
magnitude qv_⊥B, which produces a perfect circle in the transverse plane.
**Reading the distractors.** **Circular** ✗ requires v_∥ = 0. **Linear** ✗ requires
v_⊥ = 0. **Elliptical** ✗ arises from no magnetic field configuration ✓
∴ Helical.

The energy stored in an inductor is **½LI²**.
**Step 1 — write the formula.**
U = ½LI² ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
U = ½(2)(1)²
= **1 J** ✓
**Where the energy is stored.** In the **magnetic field** inside the solenoid ✓ with
energy density B²/(2µ₀) joules per cubic metre. Integrating that over the solenoid's
volume reproduces ½LI² exactly.
**Why the factor of ½.** The current builds up **gradually** from zero ✓ The back-emf
opposes it throughout, and the work done against that emf is
∫₀^I LI′ dI′ = **½LI²** ✓
Using LI² without the half - the commonest slip - gives 2 J, which is the first
distractor.
**The parallel with a capacitor.**
inductor: U = **½LI²**, energy in the **magnetic** field ✓
capacitor: U = **½CV²**, energy in the **electric** field ✓
The two are exact analogues, with current playing the part of voltage and L that of C.
**Why the energy returns when the circuit opens.** The inductor opposes the **decrease**
in current just as it opposed the increase ✓ releasing its stored joule - which is why
switching off an inductive circuit can produce a large spark at the contacts, as the
energy is dumped in a very short time.
**A worked comparison.** Doubling the current to 2 A gives
U = ½(2)(4) = **4 J** ✓ four times as much, since the energy goes as **I²**.
**Where the inductance itself comes from.**
L = µ₀n²Al ✓ for a solenoid - determined entirely by its geometry and whether it has an
iron core. The 2 H quoted here is a substantial inductance, implying many turns or a
core.
**The practical use.** Inductors smooth currents in power supplies, store energy in
switched-mode converters, and - with a capacitor - form the resonant circuits that tune
radios ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **2 J** ✗ omits the ½. **4 J** ✗ and **5 J** ✗ match no
combination of L = 2 H and I = 1 A ✓
∴ 1 J.

A cyclotron works on **any** charged particle, positive or negative - but not on a
neutral one.
**Step 1 — recall how it works.** A magnetic field bends the particle into a circle
inside two hollow **dees**, and an alternating voltage across the gap accelerates it
each time it crosses ✓ The radius grows with each kick, so the particle spirals
outward.
**Step 2 — see what is required of the particle.** It must have **charge**, so that the
magnetic field can bend it and the electric field can accelerate it ✓ Nothing in the
mechanism cares about the **sign**.
**Step 3 — see what the sign changes.** Only the **direction of circulation** ✓ A
positive particle circles one way and a negative one the other, and the accelerating
voltage must alternate in the appropriate phase. Both are perfectly workable.
**Step 4 — conclude.** A cyclotron accelerates **both positively and negatively charged
particles** ✓
**Why a neutron cannot be accelerated.** It carries **no charge**, so neither field
touches it ✓ Neutrons are produced by nuclear reactions and moderated by collisions -
never accelerated electrically.
**The resonance condition.** The cyclotron works because the period
T = 2πm/(qB) ✓
is **independent of the speed** ✓ so a fixed-frequency oscillator stays in step turn
after turn, however fast the particle becomes.
**Why electrons are not accelerated in practice.** Being so light, they become
**relativistic** after only a few hundred keV ✓ Their mass increases, the period
lengthens, and they drift out of step with the oscillator. Electrons are accelerated in
**betatrons** and **linacs** instead - but the limitation is relativistic, not one of
charge sign.
**The relativistic fix.** A **synchrocyclotron** lowers the oscillator frequency as the
particle gains mass; a **synchrotron** raises the field instead and keeps the radius
fixed ✓
**The final energy.** E = q²B²R²/(2m) ✓ set by the magnet's size and strength, which is
why high-energy machines are so large.
**Reading the distractors.** **Neutron** ✗ has no charge. **Only positive** and **only
negative** ✗ each invent a restriction the physics does not impose ✓
∴ both positively and negatively charged particles.

An electromagnetic wave travels along **Ē x B̄**, the direction of the Poynting vector.
**Step 1 — recall the geometry.** In a plane electromagnetic wave, Ē, B̄ and the
direction of propagation are **mutually perpendicular**, and they form a **right-handed
set** in that order ✓
**Step 2 — identify the direction.** The energy flows along the **Poynting vector**
S̄ = (1/µ₀)(Ē x B̄) ✓
and that is also the direction in which the wave advances.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The propagation direction is along **Ē x B̄** ✓
**Why not B̄ x Ē.** That is the **opposite** direction, since the cross product is
**anti-commutative** ✓ The order matters absolutely, and getting it right is the whole
of this question.
**A worked instance.** With Ē along +x̂ and B̄ along +ŷ:
Ē x B̄ = x̂ x ŷ = **+ẑ** ✓ the wave travels along +z.
**Why the wave cannot travel along Ē or B̄.** The fields are **transverse** - they
oscillate **perpendicular** to the direction of travel ✓ An electromagnetic wave has no
longitudinal field component at all, which is why light can be **polarised**.
**What the Poynting vector measures.** The **power per unit area** carried by the wave ✓
For sunlight at the Earth, |S̄| ≈ **1·36 kW m⁻²** - the solar constant.
**The relation between the field magnitudes.**
**E₀/B₀ = c** ✓ so the electric field is numerically some 3 x 10⁸ times the magnetic
one in SI units. Both carry **equal energy densities**, though:
½ε₀E² = B²/(2µ₀) ✓
**The radiation pressure.** Because the wave carries momentum, it exerts a pressure
S/c on an absorbing surface ✓ tiny for sunlight, about 4·6 µPa, but enough to drive a
**solar sail** and to perturb the orbits of satellites.
**A memory aid.** Point the fingers of the **right hand** along Ē, curl them towards B̄,
and the thumb gives the direction of travel ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Ē** ✗ and **B̄** ✗ are both transverse to the motion.
**B̄ x Ē** ✗ points **backwards** along the ray ✓
∴ Ē × B̄.
